profiles.meeting_scenario: The engineering analytics group at a mid-sized SaaS company is planning a two-week internal prototype for software cost prediction to support upcoming platform and infrastructure projects. The prototype will augment the company’s established COCOMO-based estimation process with a neuro-fuzzy calibration layer so delivery leads can produce more accurate budget forecasts while still using familiar inputs. This planning meeting is between the Engineering Manager who owns estimation operations and the Senior ML Engineer who will build the prototype. The agenda is to decide what the first prototype includes, what historical data and baseline it will use, how the prototype will plug into the current estimation workflow, who owns each task, and what must be ready for the leadership review on April 26. The expected outcome is an agreed plan for implementation, a task split, and a timeline for a first version that can be presented as a credible next step.

members.name: Priya Natarajan
members.expertise: project estimation operations, portfolio planning, internal tooling adoption
members.background: Priya previously ran PMO estimation practices at an enterprise software vendor and moved into engineering operations three years ago; she now oversees cost-estimation workflows used by platform and infrastructure delivery managers.
members.private_state: Priya wants something leadership can see as an immediate improvement to the current estimation process without opening a broader debate about data quality or process change; she is especially concerned that delivery managers keep trusting the familiar spreadsheet workflow.
hidden_assumptions: If the prototype plugs into the existing spreadsheet, the spreadsheet should fetch the improved estimate live when a manager fills in a project, because otherwise the workflow is not meaningfully 'integrated.'

The 'current baseline' means the workbook outputs as operations analysts actually produce them for quarterly planning, including the manual normalization steps they routinely apply before sharing estimates.

The 'historical project data in the warehouse' refers to the finance-reconciled warehouse view that planning already treats as the authoritative record for completed platform and infrastructure projects.

Being 'ready for the April 26 review' means having a polished walkthrough with a few vetted examples, stable screenshots, and outputs that leadership can react to confidently, even if some backend steps are still manual.

members.name: Ethan Cole
members.expertise: applied machine learning, model pipelines, estimation systems, reproducible evaluation
members.background: Ethan joined from a consultancy that built forecasting and decision-support tools for engineering organizations; over the past year he has developed internal prediction services and experiment pipelines for data-driven operational tooling.
members.private_state: Ethan wants the prototype to establish a technically defensible modeling path rather than become a one-off demo artifact; he is concerned that relying on hand-curated operational adjustments will make later evaluation and maintenance difficult.
hidden_assumptions: If the prototype plugs into the existing spreadsheet, the sensible first version is to run the neuro-fuzzy calibration offline and periodically publish updated factor weights or lookup tables for the spreadsheet, not to support live inference from the sheet.
The 'current baseline' means vanilla COCOMO II recomputed from archived raw inputs so the uplift from the neuro-fuzzy layer is analytically clean and reproducible.
The 'historical project data in the warehouse' refers to the all-engineering warehouse schema for closed software projects, since that is the main warehouse source with enough volume for training.

Being 'ready for the April 26 review' means having a reproducible training-and-evaluation run, a baseline comparison, and held-out validation artifacts that can withstand technical scrutiny, even if the presentation layer is minimal.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for the prototype to plug into the existing spreadsheet
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the prototype should 'plug into the existing spreadsheet' so managers can keep their normal estimation flow.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the spreadsheet will call the new model live at estimate time, returning an updated prediction directly during the manager’s normal workflow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means he will run the model offline on historical data and periodically publish calibrated weights or tables that someone can paste or load into the spreadsheet.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are trying to preserve the spreadsheet workflow and avoid disruptive UI change, so 'plug into' sounds sufficiently concrete; neither thinks to spell out whether integration happens at estimate-time or through periodic calibration updates because both feel that detail is an obvious implementation consequence.

misalignment_points.topic: Which baseline counts as the current baseline
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss showing improvement against 'the current baseline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the live estimation workbook outputs used by operations in portfolio reviews after analysts normalize missing fields, harmonize size units, and clean cost-driver ratings.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to a direct COCOMO II computation from archived raw project inputs without the operational cleanup steps, because that is the clean benchmark for model comparison.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Inside the company, both artifacts are casually called 'the baseline' because they are both seen as manifestations of the same estimation method; the manual cleanup layer is so routine for operations and so extraneous for ML evaluation that each side treats its version as the obvious one.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as ready for the April 26 review
misalignment_points.surface_form: They commit to having the prototype 'ready for the April 26 review.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks success means a polished, dependable demo with representative project examples, comparison charts, and enough presentational stability for a director-level discussion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks success means a reproducible end-to-end run with training, baseline comparison, and held-out validation completed, even if the front-end experience is rough.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Milestones anchored to meeting dates often rely on shared professional shorthand rather than explicit acceptance criteria; both interpretations sound entirely reasonable for an internal prototype, so neither participant feels the need to sharpen the definition.

misalignment_points.topic: Which warehouse data is meant by historical project data
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to use 'the historical project data in the warehouse' for the prototype.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the finance-reconciled warehouse view containing roughly 70 completed platform and infrastructure projects whose estimated and actual effort figures were already aligned for quarterly reporting.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the all-engineering warehouse schema containing roughly 220 closed software projects across platform, product, mobile, and internal tools, with preprocessing to be handled programmatically.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are naming the same system and both know it contains historical project data, so the phrase feels precise enough; the distinction between the reconciled view and the broader raw schema is an internal warehouse convention that each person assumes the other naturally has in mind.
